Particles in Action

Particles are always moving. Today: how we know they move (Brownian motion), how they spread (diffusion), how they push (gas pressure) — and how to read and draw the graphs that go with them.

PART 0 Graph toolkit

LEARN · Line graph or bar chart?
Line graph — both things are numbers that change smoothly (time, temperature)
Bar chart — one thing is a name / group (iron, wax, salt…)
LEARN · 5 rules for a good graph
1x-axis = what you change · y-axis = what you measure
2a label + unit on both axes, e.g. Time (min)
3even scale (equal steps) · graph fills more than half the grid
4points are small × marks in pencil
5one smooth best-fit line — not dot-to-dot
LEARN · Describing a pattern
Say what happens and use numbers from the graph:
“As the time increases, the temperature increases. After 2 minutes it is 34 °C and after 10 minutes it is 86 °C.”
Two kinds of exam question: describe = say what happens, with numbers · explain = say why it happens, using particles

PART 0 Reading a heating curve

LEARN
When ice is heated, its temperature goes up, then stays flat while it melts, goes up again, then stays flat while it boils. On the flat parts the energy is used to break the forces between particles, not to make them move faster — so the temperature does not rise.

PART 1 Brownian motion

LEARN
In 1827 a scientist called Robert Brown looked at pollen grains in water under a microscope. They jiggled about in a random zigzag — but nothing was touching them!
In class we see the same thing with smoke in a smoke cell.

Why does it happen?

Tiny air particles (too small to see) hit the smoke speck from all sides. The hits are uneven — more on one side — so the speck is pushed one way, then another.

Why does it matter?

It is evidence that particles really exist and are always moving. If the air is warmer, the particles move faster and the speck jiggles more.
Key words for your answers: hit / collide · uneven · random · evidence  ·  The smoke is not alive — it is being hit.
1.1EASY Describe how the smoke speck moves.
1.2MEDIUM Why does the smoke speck move?[2]

PART 2 Diffusion

LEARN
Diffusion = particles spreading out from where there are lots of them (high concentration) to where there are few (low concentration) — all by themselves, with no stirring. It happens because particles move randomly all the time.
StateSpeed of diffusionWhy
Gasfastparticles far apart and moving quickly — few things in the way
Liquidslowerparticles touching, so they keep bumping into each other
Solidalmost noneparticles stuck in fixed positions, only vibrating

Hotter = faster

Heat gives particles more energy, so they move faster and spread out sooner.

Real life

hairspray backstage after a dance show · food smell from the kitchen · a tea bag colouring water
Exam trap: when everything is evenly mixed, the particles do not stop. They keep moving — we just can't see any change.

PART 3 Gas pressure & air pressure

LEARN
Gas particles zoom around and hit the walls of their container. Each hit is a tiny push. All the pushes together make gas pressure.
The air around us is made of particles too — they push on us all the time. This is air pressure.

3 ways to increase the pressure

More particles

pump up a tyre → more hits

Hotter

orange = moving faster → hit harder & more often

Smaller space

squash it → hit walls more often
Pressure difference: if the pressure inside and outside are not the same, things get crushed or puffed up.
→
Up high the air pressure outside is low. When the plane lands, the outside air pressure is higher than inside the bottle, so the air outside pushes the bottle in.

My checklist

  • Temperature on the x-axis (what we changed), time on the y-axis (what we measured)
  • Both axes have a label and a unit — (°C) and (s)
  • The scale goes up in equal steps and the graph uses more than half the grid
  • Points are small × marks in pencil
  • One smooth curve of best fit — not dot-to-dot
  • I circled the anomalous point and did not join my line to it
